0:00–0:16

A professor fills the board. Students copy. But who is lost, and why? The professor cannot read hundreds of answers. Students wait for feedback, and passive classes make attention difficult, especially for those of us with ADHD.

Source: ai-classroom-feedback-proposal.md, Problems Addressed and Motivation; user’s classroom experience. ADHD is a design motivation based on the originator’s experience, not a claim of clinically demonstrated benefit. Classroom problem framing is the product hypothesis, not a quantified prevalence claim.

alt: Student view of the QAI prototype, showing a synthetic calculus response.

text:
0:16–0:30

QAI turns that class into active practice. Students scan a QR code, explain their reasoning or upload a photo, and get immediate, private feedback grounded in course material.

Source: ai-classroom-feedback-proposal.md, Core Workflow; README.md and demo/web/teaching.js. Original prototype screenshot embedded in submission/QAI.pptx, ppt/media/image.jpeg. Screenshot uses synthetic example work. AI feedback is formative and grounded in professor-approved material; no demonstrated learning or ADHD benefit is claimed.

text:
0:30–0:47

Professors see what to teach next. In this synthetic example, two of six answers missed the same term. QAI surfaces the misconception and suggests an explanation and a fresh question, with the professor in control.

Source: submission/classroom-evaluation.md, simulated responses 3 and 4; demo/web/sample-report.js. Two of six synthetic responses omitted the constant 8. Screenshot captured from isolated local demo, View example report. Proposed intervention and transfer question are shown in the screenshot. Professor reviews the teaching action. No measured learning gains are claimed.

0:47–1:00

Students practise instead of just watching. Professors teach to the gaps they can now see. We’re Rick and Max. QAI makes every answer a chance to improve the next lesson.

Source: ai-classroom-feedback-proposal.md, Concept, Why AI and an Application Are Needed, and Validation and Limits. This is the product value proposition. The prototype demonstrates a feedback-to-teaching workflow; classroom impact remains to be evaluated in a real tutorial.
